                      1                       MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES

                      2                            I. STATEMENT OF ISSUES TO BE DECIDED

                      3          On March 11, 2025 Plaintiff Live Oak Banking Company (“Plaintiff”) filed a lawsuit

                      4   against multiple defendants, including Bretton Sewell and Christine Sewell, both in their

                      5   individual capacity and as trustees of the Sewell Family Trust, U/A dated 8/21/03 (the “Sewell

                      6   Trust”). The lawsuit seeks, as to the Sewells and the Trust, judgement of personal liability on

                      7   guarantees of loans given by Plaintiff to defendants Trim Tech Distribution LLC and Trim Tech

                      8   Construction, Inc (collectively, the “Borrowers”).

                      9          Bretton and Christine Sewell, in their individual capacity and as trustees of the Trust, (the

                  10      “Sewell Defendants”) filed an answer on April 17, 2025, which asserted ten affirmative defenses.

                  11      The Sewell Defendants failed to make any factual allegations in support of their asserted defenses

                  12      and none of the affirmative defenses are supported by the allegations of Plaintiff’s complaint. To

                  13      the contrary, California law expressly prohibits many of the affirmative defenses raised by the

                  14      Sewell Defendants. Plaintiff thus moves this Court for an order striking those ten affirmative

                  15      defenses under Fed. R. Civ. Proc. 12(f) (“Rule 12(f)”) as insufficiently pled and otherwise

                  16      unjustified under law.

                  17         II. SUBSTANTIVE ALLEGATIONS OF THE COMPLAINT AND PROCEDURAL
                                                       HISTORY
                  18

                  19             In December of 2022, Plaintiff gave three loans, in the total amount of $8,750,000, to

                  20      Borrowers to finance the purchase of certain assets and to finance the operations of Borrowers.

                  21      Compl. ¶¶ 13, 16. As a condition for Plaintiff giving each loan to Borrowers, the Sewell

                  22      Defendants provided unconditional guarantees of each loan to Plaintiff (the “Guarantees”).

                  23      Compl. ¶¶ 22, 29, 35. In order to secure repayment of the Guarantees, the Sewell Defendants, as

                  24      Trustees of the Sewell Trust, provided a deed of trust (the “Guarantee Deed of Trust”) against the

                  25      real property located at 58 Deodora Drive, Atherton, CA 94027 (the “Deodora Property”).

                  26      Compl. ¶¶ 23, 30, 36.

                  27             Borrowers defaulted on their obligations under the loans. Compl. ¶ 37. On March 11,

                  28      2025, Plaintiff filed this action. As to the Sewell Defendants, the complaint brings a sole cause of

    LONG BEA CH

                                                   NOTICE OF MOTION AND MOTION TO STRIKE
                           Case 5:25-cv-02467-EKL           Document 19         Filed 05/07/25       Page 7 of 13



                      1   action for judicial foreclosure on the Deodora Property and entry of a deficiency judgment on the

                      2   Guarantees after sale. Compl. ¶¶ 74-89.

                      3          The Sewell Defendants filed and served their answer on April 17, 2025.

                      4                                            III. DISCUSSION
                      5          Rule 12(f) motions to strike are intended to avoid the “expenditure of time and money that

                      6   must arise from litigation spurious issues by dispensing with those issues prior to trial . . . .”

                      7   Sidney-Vinson v. A.H. Robins Co., 697 F.2d 880, 885 (9th Cir. 1983). Rule 12(f) provides that the

                      8   Court may strike from any pleading “any insufficient defense or any redundant, immaterial,

                      9   impertinent, or scandalous matter.” In conjunction, Fed. R. Civ. Proc. 8(b) requires a defendant to

                  10      “state in short and plain terms its defenses to each claim asserted against it.” Fed. R. Civ. Proc.

                  11      8(b)(1)(a). The Ninth Circuit has previously held that “[t]he key to determining the sufficiency of

                  12      pleading an affirmative defense is whether it gives plaintiff fair notice of the defense.” Wyshak v.

                  13      City Nat’l Bank, 607 F.2d 824, 826 (9th Cir. 1979) (analyzing under the Conley pleading

                  14      standard).

                  15             The majority of courts, including this District, consistently apply the Twombly-Iqbal

                  16      pleading standard to both claims and defenses. Vogel v. Huntington Oaks Delaware Partners,

                  17      LLC, 291 F.R.D. 438, 440 (C.D. Cal. 2013) (finding that although the Ninth Circuit has not

                  18      expressly required the plausibility standard, “the entire Northern District” and the Central District

                  19      apply it.); Barnes v. AT&T Pension Benefit Plan-Nonbargained Program, 718 F.Supp.2d 1167,

                  20      1171 (N.D. Cal. 2012); see also Powertech Tech. Inc. v. Tessera, Inc., No. C 10-945, 2012 WL

                  21      1746848, at *4 (N.D. Cal. May 16, 2012) (collecting cases). Defendants are required to bolster

                  22      their “affirmative defense with some factual support . . . .” Vogel, 291 F.R.D. at 441 (emphasis in

                  23      original). This serves to discourage “the commonplace practice of asserting every possible

                  24      affirmative defense, even those that are entirely irrelevant to a plaintiff’s claim” Id. Therefore, a

                  25      failure to provide “any facts, and instead, just alleging that the affirmative defense exists” is

                  26      insufficient, and grounds to strike the defense. Barnes, 718 F.Supp.2d at 1172-73 (striking

                  27      defenses).

                  28             In addition, “an attack on a plaintiff’s case-in-chief is not an affirmative defense.” Vogel,
M ILLER N ASH LLP
 ATTO RNEY S AT LAW                                                         -7-
    LONG BEA CH

                                                 NOTICE OF MOTION AND MOTION TO STRIKE
                           Case 5:25-cv-02467-EKL           Document 19         Filed 05/07/25      Page 8 of 13



                      1   291 F.R.D. at 442 (citing Zivkovic v. S. Cal. Edison Co., 302 F.3d 1080, 1088 (9th Cir. 2002)).

                      2   Therefore, when an “affirmative defense” is an alleged “defect in a plaintiff’s claim and not an

                      3   additional set of facts that would bar recovery notwithstanding the plaintiff’s valid prima facie

                      4   case” it is not an affirmative defense. Id. (citing Barnes, 718 F.Supp.2d at 1174.)

                      5          The Sewell Defendants pled ten affirmative defenses, all bare recitation of the doctrines,

                      6   unsupported by any facts. If any of the legally unsustainable affirmative defense are permitted to

                      7   survive, Plaintiff will be required to conduct expensive and potentially unnecessary and irrelevant

                      8   discovery, and so suffer prejudice. See Barnes, 718 F.Supp.2d at 1173. The ten affirmative

                      9   defenses present a clear failure to allege any basis for their assertion. Plaintiff addresses the flaws

                  10      of each affirmative defense in turn.

                  11      A.     First Affirmative Defense
                  12             The Sewell Defendants allege that the “complaint fails to state a claim upon which relief

                  13      can be granted.” As stated above, this is not an affirmative defense, as it is an attack on the case-

                  14      in-chief. See Vogel, 291 F.R.D. at 442. Further, the affirmative defense is unsupported by any

                  15      facts. This defense should be struck as it is a factually insufficient defense and is immaterial. See

                  16      Rule 12(f).

                  17      B.     Second Affirmative Defense
                  18             The Sewell Defendants allege that “Plaintiff’s claim are barred, in whole or in part, by the

                  19      applicable statutes of limitation.” This affirmative is unsupported by any facts supporting this

                  20      defense. The District Court for the Central District of California struck a similarly pled

                  21      affirmative defense for failure to plead facts supporting the defense. “Defendant fails to plead any

                  22      facts here regarding this defense, merely setting forth that the Action is barred by the applicable

                  23      statutes of limitations. As such, the Court finds that this affirmative defense pleads a legal

                  24      conclusion and therefore fails to give Plaintiff fair notice of the defense.” Desert Eur. Motorcars,

                  25      Ltd. v. Desert Eur. Motorcars, Inc., 2011 WL 3809933, at *3 (C.D. Cal. Aug. 25, 2011); see also

                  26      Vogel, 291 F.R.D. at 442; Barnes, 718 F.Supp.2d at 1172-73 (striking statute of limitation

                  27      defense). This Court should do the same here.

                  28

    LONG BEA CH

                           Case 5:25-cv-02467-EKL           Document 19        Filed 05/07/25      Page 9 of 13



                      1   C.     Third Affirmative Defense

                      2          The Sewell Defendants allege that “Plaintiff claims are barred under California’s anti-

                      3   deficiency status.” The Sewell Defendants identify solely California Code of Civil Procedure

                      4   sections 580a, 580b, 580d, and 580e to support this defense. The Sewell Defendants again do not

                      5   allege any factual support. None of these sections support the affirmative defense of barring a

                      6   deficiency claim.

                      7          Section 580a sets forth the procedure in which a plaintiff may seek the judicial sale of real

                      8   property and a deficiency claim after the sale. Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 580a. Plaintiff has followed

                      9   that procedure in filing this complaint. See Compl. ¶ 78. The Sewell Defendants identify no

                  10      variance by Plaintiff from the statutes procedures to support this defense.

                  11             Section Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 580b provides that a deficiency judgment may not arise if

                  12      the loan arose out of certain enumerated circumstances, such as being a purchase money loan on a

                  13      residence. Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 580b. The facts alleged in the complaint are that the Deodora

                  14      Property was given as a security to support the Sewell Defendants Guaranty. Compl. ¶¶ 23, 30,

                  15      36. Therefore, the Guarantee Deed of Trust was not part of a purchase money loan or a refinance

                  16      of one, nor are any other facts pled putting the Guarantee Deed of Trust within the exceptions of

                  17      section 580b.

                  18             Section 580d provides that a deficiency judgment may not arise when the “real property or

                  19      estate for years therein has been sold by the mortgagee or trustee under power of sale contained in

                  20      the mortgage or deed of trust.” Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 580d. Here, Plaintiff seeks a judgment of

                  21      foreclosure, not to exercise the power of sale in the deed of trust, and therefore this section does

                  22      not apply.

                  23             Finally, section 580e prohibits a deficiency judgment in the event of a short sale of owner

                  24      occupied property. Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 580e. No facts are alleged that would this defense.

                  25             This affirmative defense should be struck as factually insufficient and immaterial.

                  26      D.     Fourth Affirmative Defense

                  27             Sewell Defendants allege “Defendant is not a true third-party guarantor, but the alter ego

                  28      or principal obligor, and therefore is entitled to the same anti-deficiency protections as the

                      1   borrower.”

                      2            Under California law, “a lender may recover a deficiency judgment from a guarantor who

                      3   waives his or her antideficiency protections, even though the antideficiency statutes would bar the

                      4   lender from recovering that same deficiency from the primary borrower.” CADC/RADC Venture

                      5   2011-1 LLC v. Bradley, 235 Cal. App. 4th 775, 784 (2015). As set forth in the complaint, the

                      6   Sewell Defendants provided this waiver in their Guarantee. See See Ex. G, H, I, P, Q, U to

                      7   Compl.

                      8            California authority provides a waiver of a right under a guarantee, which the borrower

                      9   itself cannot waive, is not enforceable if it is a “sham guarantee”. This doctrine applies when “the

                  10      guarantor is the principal obligor on the debt, either because he or she personally executed the

                  11      note or deed of trust, or because the guarantor is liable for the debts of the borrower by operation

                  12      of some legal principle.” Id. at 787. However, “[w]here there is legal separation between the

                  13      borrower and guarantor, however, the guaranty is enforceable unless the loan transaction has been

                  14      structured to subvert the antideficiency laws.” Id.

                  15               Here, the allegations of the complaint are that the Borrowers are separate corporations

                  16      organized under California law. Compl. ¶¶ 4-5. A principal of a corporation is not generally liable

                  17      for the debts of the corporation. See PMC, Inc. v. Kadisha, 78 Cal. App. 4th 1368, 1379 (2000).

                  18      The Sewell Defendants do not allege any facts supporting their allegation that they are the “alter

                  19      ego or principal obligor”, nor do that allege any facts supporting their allegation that they are

                  20      entitled to certain anti-deficiency protections. Therefore, the Sewell Defendants fail to plead this

                  21      affirmative defense, and it should be struck as factually insufficient and immaterial.

                  22      E.       Fifth Affirmative Defense
                  23               The Sewell Defendants allege that “Plaintiff has failed to account for all payments,

                  24      offsets, and liquidation proceeds, resulting in an inflated balance.” Similar to Defendants’ failure

                  25      to state a claim defense, this defense appears to be an attack on the case-in-chief, and is not a true

                  26      affirmative defense. See Vogel, 291 F.R.D. at 442. Regardless, it is not supported by any factual

                  27      allegations and should be struck as factually insufficient and immaterial.

                      9          The Sewell Defendants do not identify what specific waiver of rights they allege is

                  13      unwaivable right is identified, this affirmative defense should be struck as factually insufficient

                  14      and immaterial.

                  15      G.     Seventh Affirmative Defense

                  16             The Sewell Defendants allege that “The guaranty is void or unenforceable due to lack of

                  17      consideration or failure of consideration.” However, under California law, “[w]here a suretyship

                  18      obligation is entered into at the same time with the original obligation, or with the acceptance of

                  19      the latter by the creditor, and forms with that obligation a part of the consideration to him, no

                  20      other consideration need exist.” Cal. Civ. Code § 2792. Here, the complaint alleges that the

                  21      Guarantees were entered into as the same time as the loan to Borrowers. See Exs. B, G, H, I, N, P,

                  22      Q, T, U to Compl. No factual allegations are otherwise pled to support this defense, and so it is

                  23      legally defective and should be struck as factually insufficient and immaterial.
